<reason>PRO built a genuinely strong core: an opt-in option cannot make the excluded woman worse off, universal tools cannot create rides she refuses, and the friction is opt-in wait. But the motion's decision word is "enough," and CON owned it. CON adapted to PRO's two-women distinction, showed the button fails the "woman inside" on exactly the nights supply is thin, and then exposed PRO's threshold: "any rate above the mixed-only baseline of zero" is not weighing but a refusal to weigh. CON answered both pressure questions directly and honestly (named a reliability standard, conceded a PIN ride doesn't restore the categorical refuser's trip, then argued the refusal population is shrinkable by universal tools). PRO's closing repeated "lottery she cannot lose" without engaging CON's key move that the platform, not the rider, pays for every ticket via night incentives, re-verification, and litigation exposure—i.e., the operational complexity the motion actually asks about. PRO's "imitate the product she won't use" retort and its dismissal of the "hypnotic label" were fair hits, keeping this competitive, but CON made the debate easier to decide by tying every clash back to the cost side of the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2 and its closing turn on PRO's "any rate above zero" standard—showing that one completed trip per month would clear PRO's bar, so PRO had declined to weigh "enough"—combined with reframing the "lottery she cannot lose" as one where the platform pays for every ticket. PRO never squarely answered the platform-side cost point.</best_rebuttal>
